**What the Pigeons Sounded Like**

For most of the nineteenth century, the most abundant bird in North America — by some estimates the most abundant bird on Earth — was the passenger pigeon, and it numbered in the billions. They did not fly in flocks so much as in weather. Witnesses describe flocks a mile wide that took the better part of a day to pass over a single town, the noon light going dim enough that farmers lit their lamps. The sound is what people remembered. It was not chirping. It was a roar, a rolling thunder like wind in a storm, a noise you felt in your ribs as it came toward you across the fields. In 1813 Audubon watched a flock cross Kentucky, tried counting it, and gave up when the arithmetic stopped meaning anything.

Then we shot them by the ton and cut down their forests, and by September 1, 1914, all of that sky and all of that sound had been reduced to a single elderly bird named Martha, dying on the floor of a cage at the Cincinnati Zoo. She was the last. And here is the part I find hard to shake: no one ever recorded the sound. We have skins in museum drawers and even the bird's DNA; someday someone may try to rebuild the pigeon from that code. But the noise itself — that continental thunder people stood under for thousands of years — exists in no archive on Earth. It went extinct when Martha did, and unlike the bird, it left no specimen behind. Not one second of it.

We tend to think of extinction as something that happens to animals. It also happens to sounds. Every sound is a physical event, a pressure wave born once and dying in the air within moments; only lately have we learned to catch a few. Nearly all the sound ever made on this planet has simply ceased. The nineteenth-century city was an animal sound before it was a mechanical one: tens of thousands of horses in New York alone, iron tires grinding on cobblestone, whips, braying, vendor cries, bells. An entire acoustic ocean, and it is gone. Buildings are instruments, too — every room shapes sound, and demolition destroys the instrument. When Notre-Dame burned in 2019, there was strange comfort in learning that acousticians had measured the building years earlier; its famous long reverb, its voice, survives as data even though the timber it bounced off is ash. For every measured cathedral there are a million rooms nobody thought to measure — your childhood kitchen, a grandmother's stairwell, the way sound behaved in a house that no longer exists.

And voices. Before 1860, no human voice outlived its owner. Roughly a hundred billion people had lived and died by then, and not one syllable of any of them remains. We know what Socrates said, and we even have a strange secondhand description of how it sounded — Alcibiades compared him to the pipes of Marsyas, ugly and irresistible — but the timbre itself, the grain of the man, is gone forever. Every lullaby of the Bronze Age. Every argument, every joke, every dying word. The most intimate thing about a person used to be the most perishable.

Then, in 1860, a Parisian typesetter named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville sang "Au clair de la lune" into his phonautograph, a machine that couldn't even play the sound back — it just scratched the vibrations of his voice into soot. Nearly a century and a half later, engineers worked out how to read the soot, and the first recorded human voice stumbled back to life. Since then, a few generations of voices persist. But recording only saves what it happens to catch, and recordings go extinct in their turn: wax cylinders, wire recordings, DAT tapes, formats no working machine can read. Even the machines have sounds dying. The dial-up handshake. The whine of a cathode-ray television — a mosquito-note at the edge of hearing that a whole generation heard every day of its childhood and then, one day, never again.

Occasionally we get a resurrection, or the nearest thing to it. A few years ago, paleontologists CT-scanned a sixty-six-million-year-old fossilized syrinx — the oldest vocal organ ever found, from a bird called Vegavis — printed it in plastic, and concluded it probably honked, goose-like, under Cretaceous skies long before anything human existed to flinch. Better still is Nesyamun, an Egyptian priest dead three thousand years, whose funerary inscriptions ask, in effect, that his soul be allowed to speak. Researchers scanned his preserved vocal tract, 3D-printed it, attached it to an artificial larynx, and coaxed out a single sustained vowel: his voice's ghost, one syllable long. He asked, more or less, to be heard. Three millennia later, someone with a scanner and a printer said yes.

Meanwhile, languages are going out at a rate that should alarm us the way the pigeons' collapse should have. Around seven thousand languages are spoken today, and on many estimates half will not survive the century. Each is a way of sounding — a particular set of human noises, a music of grief and jokes that exists nowhere else. You can translate words. You cannot translate the sound of a word said with love in a language that nobody speaks anymore.

Here is what steadies me, or at least points somewhere. Most sound will never be recorded, no matter how good our machines get. Rain on some village roof tonight, a laugh in a kitchen, the particular voice of someone you loved and never thought to capture — these exist exactly once, and then they are pigeons, a flock that passed and will not pass again. You cannot archive your way out of this. Preservation is rare, expensive, and fails eventually anyway; tapes shed their oxide, files corrupt. The older and humbler skill is attention. Listening, done honestly, is a form of witnessing — attending the first and final performance of things.

Somewhere above your head right now a sound is happening that will never happen again. Maybe the hum of your refrigerator, maybe traffic, maybe rain — small flocks, one moment wide. The people who ran out of their houses to look up at the pigeons didn't know they were watching the beginning of the end; they only knew the sky was full and roaring, and they looked up anyway. That is what listening is. The sky is full of sounds that will not come again, and they are passing over right now, and all we can do about it — which is also, it turns out, everything — is to be here with our ears open while they do.

**What the Pigeons Sounded Like**

For most of the nineteenth century, the most abundant bird in North America — by some estimates the most abundant bird on Earth — was the passenger pigeon, and there were billions of them. They did not fly in flocks so much as in weather. Witnesses describe flocks a mile wide that took the better part of a day to pass over a single town, birds stacked wing over wing into the sky until the noon light went dim enough that farmers lit their lamps. The sound is what people remembered. It was not chirping. It was a roar, a rolling thunder like wind in a storm or a river in flood, loud enough to drown out conversation, a noise you felt in your ribs as it came toward you across the fields. In 1813, Audubon watched one such flock cross Kentucky, tried to count it, and gave up when the arithmetic stopped meaning anything.

Then we shot them by the ton and cut down their forests, and on September 1, 1914, all of that sky and all of that sound had been reduced to a single elderly bird named Martha, dying on the floor of a cage at the Cincinnati Zoo. She was the last. And here is the part that I find hard to shake: no one ever recorded the sound. We have stuffed skins in museum drawers and even the bird's DNA, and someday someone may try to rebuild the pigeon from its code. But the noise itself — that continental thunder that people stood under for thousands of years — exists in no archive on Earth. It went extinct when Martha did, and unlike the bird, it left no specimen behind. Not one second of it.

We tend to think of extinction as something that happens to animals. It is also something that happens to sounds. Every sound is a physical event, a pressure wave that is born once and dies in the air within moments, and only lately have we learned to catch a few of them. Nearly all the sound ever made on this planet has simply ceased. The nineteenth-century city, for instance, was an animal sound before it was a mechanical one: tens of thousands of horses in New York alone, iron tires grinding on cobblestone, whips, braying, the cries of street vendors, church bells. An entire acoustic ocean, and it is gone. Buildings are instruments too — every room shapes sound, and when a room is demolished its acoustics die with it. When Notre-Dame burned in 2019, it was strange, obscure comfort to learn that acousticians had digitally measured the cathedral years earlier, so that its famous long reverb, its voice, survives as data even though the timber it bounced off is ash. For every measured cathedral there are a million rooms nobody thought to measure: your childhood kitchen, the stairwell at your grandmother's, the way sound behaved in a house that no longer exists.

And voices. Before 1860, no human voice outlived its owner. Roughly a hundred billion people had lived and died by then, and not one syllable of any of them remains. We know what Socrates said, and we even have a strange secondhand description of how it sounded — Alcibiades compared him to the pipes of Marsyas, ugly and irresistible — but the timbre itself, the actual grain of the man's voice, is gone forever. Every lullaby of the Bronze Age. Every argument, every joke, every dying word. The most intimate thing about a person used to be the most perishable.

Then, in April 1860, a Parisian typesetter named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville sang "Au clair de la lune" into his phonautograph, a machine that couldn't even play the sound back — it just scratched the vibrations of his voice into soot. Nearly a century and a half later, engineers worked out how to read the soot, and the first recorded human voice stumbled back to life. Since then, a few generations of voices persist. But recording only saves what it happens to catch, and it goes extinct in its turn: wax cylinders, wire recordings, DAT tapes, formats that no working machine can read. Even the machines have sounds going extinct. The dial-up handshake. The whine of a cathode-ray television — a high thin mosquito-note at the edge of hearing that an entire generation heard every day of its childhood and then, one day, never heard again.

Occasionally we get a resurrection, or the next thing to it. A few years ago, paleontologists CT-scanned a sixty-six-million-year-old fossilized syrinx from a bird called Vegavis, the oldest vocal organ ever found, printed it in plastic, and concluded that it probably honked — goose-like, absurd, under Cretaceous skies long before anything human existed to flinch at the noise. Better still is Nesyamun, an Egyptian priest dead three thousand years, whose funerary inscriptions ask, in effect, that his soul be allowed to speak. Researchers scanned his preserved vocal tract, 3D-printed it, attached it to an artificial larynx, and coaxed out a single sustained vowel: his voice's ghost, one syllable long. He asked, more or less, to be heard. Three millennia later, someone with a scanner and a printer said yes.

Meanwhile, languages are going out at a rate that should alarm us the way the pigeons' collapse should have. Around seven thousand languages are spoken today, and by many estimates half will not survive the century. Each one is a way of sounding — a particular set of human noises, a music of grief and jokes that exists nowhere else. You can translate words. You cannot translate the sound of a word being said with love in a language that nobody speaks anymore.

And here is the thing that finally steadies me, or at least points somewhere. Most sound will never be recorded, no matter how good our machines get. The rain on some village roof tonight, a laugh in a kitchen, the particular voice of someone you loved and never thought to capture — these exist exactly once, and then they are pigeons, a flock that passed and will not pass again. You cannot archive your way out of this. Preservation is rare, expensive, and fails eventually anyway; tapes shed their oxide, files corrupt. The older and humbler skill is attention. Listening, done honestly, is a form of witnessing — attending the first and final performance of things.

Somewhere above your head right now a sound is happening that will never happen again. Maybe it's the hum of your refrigerator, maybe traffic, maybe rain — small flocks, one moment wide. The people who ran out of their houses to look up at the pigeons didn't know they were watching the beginning of the end; they only knew the sky was full and roaring, and they looked up anyway. That is what listening is. The sky is full of sounds that will not come again, and they are passing over right now, and all we can do about it — which is also, it turns out, everything — is to be here with our ears open while they do.

**What the Pigeons Sounded Like**

For most of the nineteenth century, the most abundant bird in North America — by some estimates the most abundant bird on Earth — was the passenger pigeon, and there were billions of them. They did not fly in flocks so much as in weather. Witnesses describe flocks a mile wide that took the better part of a day to pass over a single town, birds stacked wing over wing into the sky until the noon light went dim enough that farmers lit their lamps. The sound is what people remembered. It was not chirping. It was a roar, a rolling thunder like wind in a storm or a river in flood, loud enough to drown out conversation, a noise you felt in your ribs as it came toward you across the fields. In 1813, Audubon watched one such flock cross Kentucky, tried to count it, and gave up when the arithmetic stopped meaning anything.

Then we shot them by the ton and cut down their forests, and on September 1, 1914, all of that sky and all of that sound had been reduced to a single elderly bird named Martha, dying on the floor of a cage at the Cincinnati Zoo. She was the last. And here is the part that I find hard to shake: no one ever recorded the sound. We have stuffed skins in museum drawers and even the bird's DNA, and someday someone may try to rebuild the pigeon from its code. But the noise itself — that continental thunder that people stood under for thousands of years — exists in no archive on Earth. It went extinct when Martha did, and unlike the bird, it left no specimen behind. Not one second of it.

We tend to think of extinction as something that happens to animals. It is also something that happens to sounds. Every sound is a physical event, a pressure wave that is born once and dies in the air within moments, and only lately have we learned to catch a few of them. Nearly all the sound ever made on this planet has simply ceased. The nineteenth-century city, for instance, was an animal sound before it was a mechanical one: tens of thousands of horses in New York alone, iron tires grinding on cobblestone, whips, braying, the cries of street vendors, church bells. An entire acoustic ocean, and it is gone. Buildings are instruments too — every room shapes sound, and when a room is demolished its acoustics die with it. When Notre-Dame burned in 2019, it was strange, obscure comfort to learn that acousticians had digitally measured the cathedral years earlier, so that its famous long reverb, its voice, survives as data even though the timber it bounced off is ash. For every measured cathedral there are a million rooms nobody thought to measure: your childhood kitchen, the stairwell at your grandmother's, the way sound behaved in a house that no longer exists.

And voices. Before 1860, no human voice outlived its owner. Roughly a hundred billion people had lived and died by then, and not one syllable of any of them remains. We know what Socrates said, and we even have a strange secondhand description of how it sounded — Alcibiades compared him to the pipes of Marsyas, ugly and irresistible — but the timbre itself, the actual grain of the man's voice, is gone forever. Every lullaby of the Bronze Age. Every argument, every joke, every dying word. The most intimate thing about a person used to be the most perishable.

Then, in April 1860, a Parisian typesetter named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville sang "Au clair de la lune" into his phonautograph, a machine that couldn't even play the sound back — it just scratched the vibrations of his voice into soot. Nearly a century and a half later, engineers worked out how to read the soot, and the first recorded human voice stumbled back to life. Since then, a few generations of voices persist. But recording only saves what it happens to catch, and it goes extinct in its turn: wax cylinders, wire recordings, DAT tapes, formats that no working machine can read. Even the machines have sounds going extinct. The dial-up handshake. The whine of a cathode-ray television — a high thin mosquito-note at the edge of hearing that an entire generation heard every day of its childhood and then, one day, never heard again.

Occasionally we get a resurrection, or the next thing to it. A few years ago, paleontologists CT-scanned a sixty-six-million-year-old fossilized syrinx from a bird called Vegavis, the oldest vocal organ ever found, printed it in plastic, and concluded that it probably honked — goose-like, absurd, under Cretaceous skies long before anything human existed to flinch at the noise. Better still is Nesyamun, an Egyptian priest dead three thousand years, whose funerary inscriptions ask, in effect, that his soul be allowed to speak. Researchers scanned his preserved vocal tract, 3D-printed it, attached it to an artificial larynx, and coaxed out a single sustained vowel: his voice's ghost, one syllable long. He asked, more or less, to be heard. Three millennia later, someone with a scanner and a printer said yes.

Meanwhile, languages are going out at a rate that should alarm us the way the pigeons' collapse should have. Around seven thousand languages are spoken today, and by many estimates half will not survive the century. Each one is a way of sounding — a particular set of human noises, a music of grief and jokes that exists nowhere else. You can translate words. You cannot translate the sound of a word being said with love in a language that nobody speaks anymore.

And here is the thing that finally steadies me, or at least points somewhere. Most sound will never be recorded, no matter how good our machines get. The rain on some village roof tonight, a laugh in a kitchen, the particular voice of someone you loved and never thought to capture — these exist exactly once, and then they are pigeons, a flock that passed and will not pass again. You cannot archive your way out of this. Preservation is rare, expensive, and fails eventually anyway; tapes shed their oxide, files corrupt. The older and humbler skill is attention. Listening, done honestly, is a form of witnessing — attending the first and final performance of things.

Somewhere above your head right now a sound is happening that will never happen again. Maybe it's the hum of your refrigerator, maybe traffic, maybe rain — small flocks, one moment wide. The people who ran out of their houses to look up at the pigeons didn't know they were watching the beginning of the end; they only knew the sky was full and roaring, and they looked up anyway. That is what listening is. The sky is full of sounds that will not come again, and they are passing over right now, and all we can do about it — which is also, it turns out, everything — is to be here with our ears open while they do.
